Yes. 

The ending of the story feels natural, earned, and deeply satisfying because it resolves both the internal psychological conflict and the interpersonal tension established at the beginning. 

Throughout the narrative, Daniel is haunted by a recurring dream of an unused flat where his ex-wife, Rachel, waits. Through finding the old boathouse keys, Daniel realizes the dream isn't about wanting Rachel back, but rather about having locked away a joyful, spontaneous version of himself in the box of a marriage that "Didn't Work." Furthermore, his current partner, Isabel, struggles with being overly "reasonable" and guarded, a trait that contributed to the end of her own past marriage.

The final scene on the river brings all these threads together. By taking a canoe out with Isabel, Daniel reclaims that lost, unguarded part of himself and integrates it into his present life, while Isabel allows herself to be clumsy and unguarded in public ("with no one to be reasonable for"). Daniel mentally lays the dream to rest—imagining Rachel finally leaving the flat—and focuses entirely on moving forward with Isabel. The ending directly delivers on the emotional and thematic buildup of the entire piece, providing a complete sense of closure.
